events.title: Buchanan Lecture with Jenn Brophy | Programmable memory as a tool for plant genome engineering
events.description: Transkingdom transfer of DNA from Agrobacterium to plants is a stunning biological feat and the basis of the most widely used tool for introducing new DNA into plants. Yet despite decades of use, fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of Agrobacterium-mediated DNA transfer, particularly the dynamics and mechanisms of transferred DNA (T-DNA) integration into the plant genome. These gaps have limited our ability to reliably control transgene insertion. We developed T-SWITCH (T-DNA Sensing With Integrase CHassis), a transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana line that can be used to independently measure T-DNA delivery and integration after Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, to dissect these processes. Using T-SWITCH, we found that most transformation variables, including DNA repair factors, Agrobacterium virulence proteins, promoter choice, and vector architecture, act on T-DNA delivery, not integration. We find that ~17% of T-DNA delivery events do not result in T-DNA integration. Building on this insight, we use T-SWITCH to achieve integration-free genome editing, producing heritable mutations without Cas9 T-DNA in the genome in a single generation. In a related project we build synthetic genetic circuits that can sense and record specific biological events to achieve greater control over gene expression across the Arabidopsis root system. In Arabidopsis, a single primary root gives rise to secondary (lateral) roots, which subsequently branch into tertiary roots to form an increasingly complex root network over the plant's life. But because these branch types share the same core regulatory machinery, they have been impossible to control independently. We developed a synthetic genetic "counter" that can record repeated developmental events and enable independent control over gene expression across root types. The system successfully counts to two in heterozygous plants, and we discuss ongoing work to apply it for manipulation of root traits. Together, these systems show how synthetic circuits that record biological events can be used to understand or engineer previously inaccessible plant processes.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Mathew Hauer and Tyler McCormick: "AI in Demography"
events.description: Mathew E. Hauer is the Charles B. Nam Associate Professor of Sociology at Florida State University, Assistant Director of the Center for Demography and Population Health, and the Head of AI Agent Development at Aaru, a company focused on artificial intelligence and simulation (https://aaru.com/). His research lies at the intersection of demography, migration, population projections, and climate change, with particular expertise in modeling future population dynamics under climate stress. His work on climate migration and population vulnerability has earned numerous prestigious accolades, including the 2024 Early Achievement Award (https://www.populationassociation.org/about/annual-awards/early-achievement-award#:~:text=The%20Early%20Achievement%20award%20recognizes,scholars%20who%20received%20their%20Ph.) from the Population Association of America and the 2023 Cozzarelli Prize (http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/pnas-cozzarelli-2022.html) from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, and is a finalist for the 2025 Cozzarelli Prize and the Max Planck-Humboldt Research Award. He is a two-time recipient of the E. Walter Terrie Award (https://www.sda-demography.org/Terrie-Award) for excellence in applied demography, and his dissertation on sea-level rise and human migration has accumulated over 1,500 citations since 2016. Dr. Hauer's research has significantly shaped our understanding of climate change's demographic impacts, from sea-level rise displacement to temperature extremes and coastal flooding. His work has been featured in over 800 media outlets worldwide, including the New York Times, The Guardian, Time Magazine, National Geographic, and the Washington Post. Before joining FSU, he spent nearly a decade directing the Applied Demography Program at the University of Georgia. Tyler McCormick's work develops statistical models for inference and prediction in scientific settings where data are sparsely observed or measured with error, with a particular focus on measuring and understanding human behavior. His recent projects include estimating features of social networks (e.g. the degree of clustering or how central an individual is) using data from standard surveys, inferring a likely cause of death (when deaths happen outside of hospitals) using reports from surviving caretakers, and quantifying & communicating uncertainty in predictive models for global health policymakers. He holds a Ph.D. in Statistics (with distinction) from Columbia University and is the recipient of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award, NIH Career Development (K01) Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Program Award, and a Google Faculty Research Award. Currently, he is a Professor of Statistics and Sociology at the University of Washington, where he is also a core faculty member in the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences and a Senior Data Science Fellow at the eScience Institute. During the 2019-2020 academic year Tyler was a Visiting Faculty Researcher at Google People+AI Research (PAIR). Tyler is the former Editor of the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics (JCGS) and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association. Tyler is currently a member of the Committee on Applied and Theoretical Statistics at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine. More information on Tyler's work is here: https://thmccormick.github.io (https://thmccormick.github.io/).

events.title: Shigehiro Oishi | Specialization and Its Discontent: Implications for Curiosity and Well-Being
events.location: Berkeley Way West (2121 Berkeley Way), Room 1102
events.description: Institute of Personality and Social Research ColloquiumShigehiro Oishi, Marshall Field IV Distinguished Service Professor, Department of Psychology, University of Chicago; 2026-27 Fellow, Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS), Stanford University.Specialization and Its Discontent: Implications for Curiosity and Well-Being Division of labor (specialization) is widely considered a cornerstone of modern productivity, yet its potential psychological costs are not well understood. We examined whether division of labor reduces curiosity–the motivation to explore and learn new things. Across four experiments (N = 821), participants who work, or are expected to work, in divided labor settings showed lower curiosity than those who work in undivided settings. Analyses of three large cross-sectional datasets and one longitudinal panel (N = 320,119) showed that similar patterns generalized across countries, industries, economic contexts, and personality profiles. Together, these findings suggest that, as work becomes more divided, people's motivation to explore and learn new things may diminish. Shigehiro Oishi is the Marshall Field IV Distinguished Service Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2023). He received his B.A. at International Christian University in Tokyo, Ed. M at Teachers College, Columbia University, and Ph.D. at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 2000. He taught at the University of Minnesota (2000-2004), Columbia University (2018-2020), and the University of Virginia (2004-2018; 2020-2022) before joining UChicago (2022-). He won the 2017 Society of Experimental Social Psychology Career Trajectory Award, the 2018 Carol and Ed Diener Award from the Society for Personality and Social Psychology, and the 2021 Outstanding Achievement Award for Advancing Cultural Psychology. His research focuses on culture, social ecology, and well-being. His lab is particularly interested in asking questions surrounding the concept of well-being (e.g. "what is a good life?"), the predictors of well-being (e.g. "what are the predictors of a good life?"), and the consequences of well-being (e.g. "are there benefits to a happy/meaningful/psychologically rich life?"). Furthermore, he is interested in how the concepts, the predictors, and the consequences of well-being might differ across cultures. Additionally, his research explores socio-ecological conditions that are detrimental or conducive to well-being (e.g., income inequality, residential mobility, walkability).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Ore Carmi [Tel: 510-642-5050; Email: orecarmi@berkeley.edu] with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Real Estate Populism: Urban Spectacles and the Ecological Origins of Bukelismo in El Salvador
events.description: This talk explores the geography of authoritarian populism in El Salvador. It focuses on the case of Nuevo Cuscatlán, a semi-rural town in the periphery of San Salvador where President Nayib Bukele served as mayor between 2012 and 2015. I examine how Bukele crafted his profile as a promising politician by using the urbanizing landscape as a stage for a populist media spectacle. Promoted through the name of "The New City," this spectacle portrayed the mayor as the inventor of a "new development model" capable of reconciling gentrification with longstanding working-class demands. Drawing on urban political ecology and critical agrarian studies, I demonstrate that Bukele's early political success rested on the use of land and water as political assets. This use consisted of two main practices: 1. The extraction of revenue from real estate capital through zoning and land-based compensations, and 2. The financing of public water infrastructure in a context of growing scarcity. The progressive appearance of these policies diverted attention from what was in reality a silent process of territorial dispossession whose delayed impacts reflect in current patterns of deforestation, water grabbing, and mass evictions. Dr. Julio Gutiérrez is an anthropologist and political ecologist from El Salvador. He specializes in urban political ecology and critical development studies, with a research focus on urban extractivism, land politics, and the geographies of financialization.

Talk Summary: How can we live with greater clarity, resilience, and compassion in a rapidly changing world? In this interactive "Casual Conversation," Venerable Pomnyun Sunim invites students and community members to openly explore questions about stress, relationships, career uncertainty, emotional wellbeing, social conflict, and the search for meaning in modern life. Known for his practical and accessible teaching style, Venerable Pomnyun Sunim responds directly to audience questions with insight, humor, and compassion. Rather than offering abstract religious doctrine, he shares practical wisdom grounded in Buddhist philosophy and decades of humanitarian and social engagement. The conversation may also touch on broader topics including mindfulness, sustainable living, peacebuilding, social responsibility, and how individuals can contribute positively to society while maintaining inner balance and freedom. This event is open to people of all backgrounds, beliefs, and levels of familiarity with Buddhism. Speaker Bio: Venerable Pomnyun Sunim is a highly respected Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhist monk, humanitarian leader, author, and founder of Jungto Society, an international volunteer-based organization dedicated to spiritual practice, social engagement, environmental sustainability, and peacebuilding. He is widely recognized for his accessible and deeply engaging public dialogues known as "Casual Conversations" (즉문즉설), where he responds spontaneously to audience questions about everyday life challenges. His teachings focus on practical wisdom, emotional clarity, compassion, and personal responsibility, making them highly relevant across cultural, academic, and professional communities. Venerable Pomnyun Sunim has delivered talks and interactive sessions at leading academic institutions including Harvard University, Columbia University, UCLA, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Toronto, and other universities across North America and Asia. He has also spoken with professionals at organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank, and global technology companies including Google. In 2002, he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award, often regarded as Asia's Nobel Prize, in recognition of his humanitarian work, peacebuilding efforts, and contributions to socially engaged Buddhism.

events.title: Alex Hack | The Black Body and its Many Histories: Corroborating Black Health and the Death of Medgar Evers (CRG Forum Series)
events.description: CRG Forum Series*The Black Body and its Many Histories: Corroborating Black Health and the Death of Medgar Evers withAlex Hack, UC President's & Andrew W. Mellon Postdoctoral Fellow, Departments of Gender Studies and English, University of California, Los Angeles The 1963 assassination of Medgar Evers and the many accounts that followed demonstrate the ambivalent nature of racial trauma and the ways in which patient circumstance is hidden, shaped, and dispersed via fact, feeling, and social bias. The lack of verifiability of the circumstances surrounding the death of such an influential civil rights leader speaks to a larger problem that continues within the American healthcare system: its inability to recognize more holistic and collaborative forms of evidence, especially those less interested in hegemonic knowledge, "genetic predisposition," or formulaic concerns. Taking this into account, I incorporate my father's ICU medical records, placing the supposedly "factual" nature of these documents in conversation with my own experience—ultimately looking to question the methods by which grounded understanding and familial knowledge are wiped away to make room for the "objective." Working within the rich tradition of Black feminists who have made strides to consider the body and its information, I utilize Sylvia Wynter's discussion of the programming power of language and Audre Lorde's own autotheory of illness to examine how ambiguity and a continued lack of understanding intractably remain within hegemonic health systems.Event hosted by the Center for Race and Gender (https://crg.berkeley.edu/), and co-sponsored by the Departments of African American Studies (https://africam.berkeley.edu/) and Gender & Women's Studies (https://gws.berkeley.edu/).*Lunch provided on a first-come, first-served basis. **If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

Ideally, to contribute to and enhance understanding, participants will come with current and/or previous people management experience. Trust is at the heart of every relationship, and it's especially critical in the workplace. In fact, the primary factor affecting employee turnover is whether or not a trusting relationship was developed between the manager and the employee. This workshop teaches how to build trust to increase engagement, creativity, and commitment. Based on 30 years of research, The Ken Blanchard Companies have developed a simple, yet powerful, trust model that provides a common language and framework, focused on the specific behaviors that build trust. By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to: *Describe the impact of behaviors on building and eroding trust *Identify aspects that need attention to build and maintain trusting relationships *Use tools to improve, or even rebuild trust when it is broken *Maintain a safe environment where employees know their leaders mean them no harm

events.title: Joanna Kelley - Navigating the Seasons: Unraveling the Genomic Basis of Hibernation in Brown Bears
events.description: Hibernation in bears involves a suite of seasonally reversible metabolic and physiological changes. Revealing the mechanisms underlying the reversible physiology of hibernation could have applications to both human and animal health as hibernation is often associated with disease-like states. Changes in hibernation are driven in part by sweeping changes in gene expression in multiple tissues. We determined the seasonal transcriptional changes occurring in brown bears (Ursus arctos horribilis). We continue to study the higher-level regulatory mechanisms involved in the emergence from hibernation. Moreover, we explore the population genetics of brown bears in North America and discuss implications for conservation.

events.title: Adrien Peyrache - Orienting memory during wake and sleep
events.description: The head-direction (HD) circuit, an upstream provider of orientation signals for navigation, maintains coherent internal orientation memory that stays stable within each environment for weeks. During non-REM sleep, when hippocampal trajectories are replayed for memory formation, HD cells remain coordinated and directly influence this hippocampal replay. This suggests the HD system conveys a "virtual" orientation signal to support memory replay, with the thalamus appearing to play a crucial role in generating it. Overall, the HD system supplies the hippocampus and associated structures with a coherent, possibly lifelong-stable signal maintained across brain states to support spatial navigation and memory formation.

events.title: BTS Army: Forever We Are Young - Film Screening and Conversation with Directors Grace Lee and Patty Ahn
events.location: Sutardja Dai Hall, Banatao Auditorium, Room 310, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker/s: Grace Lee (Director/Producer), Patty Ahn (University of California, San Diego) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin exactly at the scheduled time of 4:00 PM. Film Summary: From Seoul to Los Angeles, Texas to Mexico City, BTS ARMY is everywhere. BTS ARMY: FOREVER WE ARE YOUNG dives into the passionate fandom that catapulted 21st century pop icons BTS into a global household name. We meet fans at a BTS-focused ReactorCon in Lewisville, Texas, a dance instructor in Seoul who teaches BTS choreography, and fans who've been organizing since 2013 to help BTS dominate the charts. Defying stereotypes of pop fans as screaming teens, ARMY is an intergenerational, culturally savvy, and socially active movement that is as diverse as the world itself. The film captures the powerful spirit of activism and collectivity that make ARMY a symbol of hope and unity in our ever-fractured world. FOREVER WE ARE YOUNG is made BY ARMY FOR ARMY. The film centers on the fans themselves and celebrates their creativity, resilience, and deep emotional connection to the group. Though rooted in fandom, the film explores universal themes of belonging, identity, and self-love. Speaker Bios: Grace Lee recently directed and produced BTS Army: Forever We Are Young, which was released in cinemas worldwide in 2025. Other credits include Peabody winning PBS series ASIAN AMERICANS as well as And She Could be Next, about women of color transforming U.S. politics and civic engagement which aired on POV. Other credits include the Peabody-winning American Revolutionary: The Evolution of Grace Lee Boggs, The Grace Lee Project, K-TOWN'92, an interactive project about the 1992 Los Angeles civil unrest and the podcast Viewers Like Us. She co-founded Asian American Documentary Network and is a member of AMPAS Documentary branch. Patty Ahn (they/them) is a filmmaker and Associate Teaching Professor in the Communication Department at the University of California, San Diego. Their research and teaching specialize in K-Pop's growing global influence, especially in the U.S. More broadly, they work at the intersection of popular music, Media Industries, and critical race and gender studies. Their academic work has been published in Discourse, Cinema Journal, Social Text, and FlowTV.org. They have also worked as a creative producer at various music production companies. More recently, they co-edited an academic volume on BTS and are currently working on a new documentary project about K-Pop's intersection with Black music culture.

events.title: Paola Bacchetta | Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances
events.description: A talk by Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta), Professor and the Chair of the Department of Gender and Women's Studies, on her new book, Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances (https://www.dukeupress.edu/co-motion), that offers a fresh framework for understanding how feminist and queer coalitions take shape across differences and how collective movements can transform prevailing ideas about power, identity, and political agency.AnganaP. Chatterji, Founding Chair, Political Conflict, Gender, and People's Rights Initiative, Center for Race and Gender, and Research Anthropologist, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Sept 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: In Co-Motion (https://www.dukeupress.edu/co-motion), theorist Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta) proposes a new lexicon for analyzing power, subjects and alliances. Employing what she calls 'theory-assemblages' to describe how diverse theoretical and political approaches inspire movements and produce different kinds of alliances, Bacchetta engages the inseparability of power relations—such as colonialism, capitalism, racism, caste, misogyny, and speciesism—and how their combinations, operability, and the analyses they require, shift in different contexts and lives of subjects. Focusing on France, India, Italy, and the US from the 1970s to the present, Co-Motion addresses a wide activist, artivist, and social movement archive— group statements, banners, pamphlets, graffiti, posters, poetry, sit-ins, films, art exhibits—to think and feel with the many ways that people, historically and today, come together to act. Through her expansive engagement with varied bodies of scholarship, sites of analysis, and kinds of reading, Bacchetta offers new approaches to analyze, confront, and transforming power, and to enact freedom.About the Author:Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta) is Professor and the Chair of the Department of Gender and Women's Studies at University of California, Berkeley. She is a critical theorist whose research focuses on gender, sexuality, colonialism, race, religion, capitalism, Empire, and other relations of power, along with local, translocal to transnational feminist and queer activism. She also works on right-wing movements, gender and sexuality. Her areas of specialization are India, France, the U.S., Brazil and Italy. Dr. Bacchetta is the author or contributing co-editor of the following book length works: Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances (Durham: Duke University Press, 2026); Fatema Mernissi for Our Times (with Minoo Moallem, Syracuse University Press, 2025); Global Raciality: Empire, Postcoloniality, and Decoloniality, (with Sunaina Maira and Howard Winant, New York: Routledge, 2019); Femminismi Queer Postcoloniali (with Laura Fantone. Verona, Italy: Ombre Corte, 2015); Gender in the Hindu Nation (Delhi, India: Women Ink, 2004); Right-Wing Women: From Conservatives to Extremists around the World (with Margaret Power. New York: Routledge; , 2002); Textes du Mouvement Lesbien en France, 1970-2000 (with Claudie Lesselier, DVD, 2011). Dr. Bacchetta has published over 90 professional journal articles and book chapters on her research, in English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Arabic, Brazilian Portuguese and Danish. She has lectured widely within the U.S., and in Western Europe, Eastern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, Brazil and South Asia. Dr. Bacchetta is the recipient of many awards and and grants including Fulbright, Mellon, multiple different kinds of European Union grants, Peder Sather Research Fund, and the France-Berkeley Fund. She has been a postdoctoral scholar in the USA at Harvard University and the Five College Women's Studies Research Center, in France at École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales and Université de Paris 3, and in Brazil at Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (Florianópolis) and Universidade Federal de Bahia (Salvador, Bahia). events.title: Ken Raymond Lecture
events.description: Mike Pluth, Professor, University of OregonChemical Tool for Investigating Biological Sulfur and Selenium SpeciesSulfur and selenium occupy a unique position at the interface of inorganic chemistry, redox chemistry, and biology, where changes in oxidation state, speciation, and metal coordination can profoundly alter reactivity. Understanding the fundamental chemistry of reactive S and Se species therefore provides a framework for connecting molecular structure and bonding to their roles in complex biological environments. Biological sulfur metabolism is often framed around H2S as both a metabolic product and signaling species. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that persulfides (RSSH) and related dichalcogenides serve as central intermediates in sulfur trafficking, redox buffering, and enzymatic sulfur-transfer reactions. Despite their growing importance, the fundamental chemical properties that govern the reactivity, stability, and biological fate of these species remain poorly defined. This presentation will highlight recent efforts from our group to prepare and use isolable sulfur and selenium dichalcogenides to establish fundamental structure-reactivity relationships relevant to bioinorganic S/Se chemistry. Examples will include intrinsic dichalcogenide reaction chemistry, synthetic metal-persulfide model complexes, and studies showcasing how coordination to Lewis-acidic metal centers can modulate dichalcogenide electronic structure and reactivity. Together, these studies establish fundamental chemical principles for understanding sulfur and selenium transfer, provide molecular-level insight into metalloenzyme-mediated sulfur trafficking and oxidation pathways, and highlight how coordination chemistry can be used to interrogate the broader chemical landscape of sulfur metabolism.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Construction Inspection of Traffic Signals
events.description: Description Traffic signal construction is a critical component of roadway infrastructure that demands precision, adherence to standards, and proactive oversight. For inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers, success depends not only on understanding how systems are built but also on recognizing when installation deviates from plans, specifications, or best practices. Minor issues such as improper wiring, inadequate grounding, or ineffective traffic control can introduce safety risks, trigger costly rework, and increase agency liability. This intensive online course is designed to prepare participants for what they will encounter in the field when overseeing traffic signal construction. While the course does not focus on signal design, it provides essential exposure to design elements from an inspector's and owner's perspective. It is intended to help participants understand how design intent is translated into constructed systems and how to verify that the work is completed correctly, safely, and in compliance with Caltrans Standard Plans and Specifications. Participants can expect practical, field-oriented instructions on inspecting and evaluating key signal system components, including conductors and cables, signal heads, controller cabinets, grounding systems, and pedestrian and vehicle detection technologies. The course also emphasizes plan interpretation at a level appropriate for oversight roles. Participants will learn what to look for in the plans, how to identify inconsistencies, and how to apply sufficient technical understanding to assess compliance without performing design work. In addition, the course addresses coordination with contractors, construction documentation, and communication practices that support CIP delivery and protect agencies throughout project implementation. Through real-world case studies, participants will gain insight into common construction challenges, effective inspection strategies, and documentation approaches that stand up to scrutiny. Led by experienced industry professionals, this course equips inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers with the practical knowledge and judgment needed to confidently oversee traffic signal construction by bridging the gap between design intent and successful field execution. Topics IncludeSignal Plan Interpretation & Pre-Construction Activities Reading and understanding traffic signal plans Site assessments and preparatory inspections Electrical and Structural Installation Electrical service installation procedures Standards for pedestals, posts, and mounting hardware Bonding and grounding requirements Conduit and Cabling Systems Conduit installation and layout Cable splicing and termination Pull box installation and accessibility Traffic Signal Components Installation of signal heads, brackets, and supporting appurtenances Vehicle and pedestrian detector systems Pedestrian Safety & Americans with Disability Act (ADA) Signal controller cabinet assembly and configuration Construction Close-Out & Asset Management Maintenance considerations during and after construction Salvage and reuse of components Integration of new technology and smart signal components What You Will Learn By attending this class, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the full lifecycle of traffic signal construction-from interpreting signal plans and preparing for construction, to installing electrical systems, conduit, and signal components. Attendees will learn industry best practices for ensuring proper bonding, grounding, and splicing, as well as techniques for setting up signal heads, controllers, and detection systems. The course also covers maintenance strategies, salvage procedures, and the integration of modern signal technologies. Through this training, attendees will be equipped with the practical knowledge and field-based insights necessary to effectively inspect, manage, and support the delivery of safe and compliant traffic signal projects. Who Should Attend Ideal for traffic signal technicians, engineering inspectors, electrical contractors, junior engineers, and traffic signal engineers involved in the design, oversight, or inspection of signal infrastructure projects.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jeffrey Seeman, Visiting Research Scientist, University of RichmondWas Plagiarism Involved in the Woodward-Hoffmann Rules? In 1981, Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry "for their theories, developed independently, concerning the course of chemical reactions". Had R. B. Woodward (1917 – 1979) lived two years longer, he would surely have received his second Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his contributions to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules. In the March 29, 2004, issue of Chemical & Engineering News, E. J. Corey wrote in his Priestley Medal Address, "On May 4, 1964, I suggested to my colleague R. B. Woodward a simple explanation involving the symmetry of the perturbed (HOMO) molecular orbitals for the stereoselective cyclobutene/1,3-butadiene and 1,3,5-hexatriene/cyclohexadiene conversions that provided the basis for the further development of these ideas into what became known as the Woodward-Hoffmann rules." Letters between Corey and Hoffmann in 1981 and 1984 and other relevant information will be shown and discussed. This seminar will focus on responsible conduct of science and the practice of science in today's complex and fast moving scientific, academic, and political environments.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Robust Statistics for Monetary Non-Neutrality in Menu Cost Economies"
events.description: Abstract: The first two entries of the IRF of firm-level prices to firm-level marginal cost shocks are numerically sufficient to recover the generalized Phillips curve Jacobian in a wide class of pricing models. This result is exact in Calvo and in the Gertler-Leahy menu cost model, is numerically accurate for a broad set of CalvoPlus parameterizations, including those in Golosov and Lucas (2007) and Nakamura and Steinsson (2010), and it works in models with strategic complementarities. Our approach recovers the rigidity parameter of the synthetic Calvo model that approximates the Jacobian of the unknown true menu-cost data generating process, operationalizing the numerical equivalence results in Auclert et al. (2024). This virtual Calvo hazard may be arbitrarily different from the frequency of price changes computed in a dataset of firm-level prices.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Robert Baker, Timashev Professorship in Chemical Physics, Ohio State UniversityElucidating Charge, Spin, and Solvation Dynamics at Electrochemical InterfacesNearly all energy conversion and information processing technologies rely on charge and spin transport in systems that are far from equilibrium. The goal to understand and control these processes motivates the need to develop methods to probe the underlying electron dynamics in functional materials on the relevant scales of time and space. To meet this challenge, we utilize high harmonic generation to produce extreme ultraviolet (XUV) light with femtosecond to attosecond pulse durations. Like X-ray absorption, XUV spectroscopy is element specific, providing chemical details of individual elements in complex materials. To extend this technique to study electron dynamics at surfaces, we have pioneered XUV reflection as a surface sensitive analog of XUV absorption. This method now enables direct observation of interfacial charge and spin transport with surface sensitivity, ultrafast time resolution, and unprecedented chemical specificity. This talk will present recent measurements using linearly and circularly polarized XUV light, which show how spin polarized electron transport increases water splitting efficiency in yttrium iron garnet (Y3Fe5O12) by more than an order of magnitude compared to widely studied hematite (α-Fe2O3) through the formation of spin-locked magnon-polarons and how angular momentum exchange between electrons and chiral phonons generates ultrafast spin polarization in chiral semiconductors. Finally, this talk will describe nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy of interfacial electric fields, which mediate charge transfer kinetics during electrochemical catalysis, and show how together these spectroscopic methods provide a detailed understanding of the molecular features of interfaces that govern non-equilibrium reaction dynamics.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Knowing better, doing better? Lessons for police reform from a developmental science law enforcement training program
events.organizer: Institute for the Study of Societal Issues
events.description: Youth commonly encounter police in their daily lives, and one of every four arrests in the United States is of a person under the age of 25. Compared to adults, interactions between youth and police more often lead to use of force and physical and emotional harm—harms that disproportionately burden the economically poor and Black youth who come into contact with police at relatively high rates. Debates over the proper role of police in managing young people have existed for over a century, yet there is little consensus as to what the ideal relationship between youth and law enforcement should be, systematic efforts to alter these relationships have had limited or even perverse results, and contemporary phenomena (e.g., social media, teen "takeovers," and changing parenting approaches) bring new challenges to youth-police relations and reform efforts. This talk brings together developmental science, historical sociology, anti-carceral perspectives, and primary research to make sense of "what works" (and doesn't work) in implementing police reform for youth. To do so, Jacobs and co-investigator Murray will draw on diverse data sources, including interviews (n = 26) and surveys with police (n = 111), and non-participant observation of police training (154 hours) in a California county, sharing preliminary findings from an ongoing, mixed methods, multi-site and multi-year impact and implementation study of a law enforcement training program that seeks to improve police-youth interactions. Implications for scholarship and intervention will be discussed.Leah Jacobs, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the School of Social Work at the University of Pittsburgh, where she leads the Anti-carceral Social Work Research Lab and the Public Social Work Research Collaborative. Her scholarship is at the intersection of social welfare, criminal legal, and community mental health policy and intervention. In these areas, she studies social problems and responses to them, with particular attention to the disproportionate involvement of Black and economically poor Americans, and people diagnosed with serious mental illnesses, in carceral and coercive systems. Her current work focuses on the relationship between social work and policing, and on life-affirming alternatives to carceral and coercive interventions, especially those that prevent system involvement and build capacity among members of minoritized groups. She holds a BS in Psychology from Northeastern University, an MA in Urban and Environmental Policy and Planning/Child Development from Tufts University, and an MSW/PhD in Social Welfare from UC Berkeley, where she was a Graduate Fellow at the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues.

events.title: Frank Bösch | The "New Jews": (Post-)Soviet Migration and the Reinvention of Jewishness in Germany since 1990
events.description: Jewish communities in East and West Germany were small and aging in the late 1980s. Only about 400 Jews remained in the Jewish communities of the GDR. This changed dramatically after 1990. Over the subsequent 15 years, about 220,000 Jews and their relatives emigrated from the former Soviet Union to Germany. Frank Bösch's presentation analyzes how the country that perpetrated the Holocaust became one of the foremost destinations for Jewish migration, alongside Israel and the United States, becoming the leading destination in the early 2000s. Based on extensive archival research and interviews, the presentation shows how German officials shaped this exceptional immigration program by granting work permits and social security benefits, and how migrants with Soviet backgrounds experienced life in Germany and reshaped their identities. The talk also examines the agency of those seeking to leave the Soviet Union, exploring the strategies they used to emigrate to Germany and how they circumvented bureaucratic rules. The migration process also generated many conflicts, including with established German Jewish communities, which led to new hybrid identities. At least in the 1990s, expectations on all sides remained unfulfilled. Jewish migration thus became a story of broken expectations. Frank Bösch is Professor of Twentieth-Century European History at the University of Potsdam and Director of the Leibniz Centre for Contemporary History Potsdam (ZZF), a leading research institute in Germany. He is the author of numerous influential books, including several bestsellers. His most recent book examines Germany's relations with autocracies (Deals mit Diktaturen, 2024). Previous publications have explored topics such as the history of the Christian Democratic Party (Die Adenauer CDU, 2001), the changing influence of media (Mass Media and Historical Change, 2015), and global turning points in the late 1970s (Zeitenwende 1979, 2019). He is currently writing a book on Jewish migration from the Soviet Union to Germany between 1970 and 2005, tentatively titled The New Jews in Germany. The Gerda Henkel Lecture Tours were established in 2018 by the Pacific Office of the German Historical Institute Washington in cooperation with the Gerda Henkel Foundation. Each year, the series brings leading German historians to the West Coast to present their latest research and to engage in conversations with diverse academic and public audiences across North America.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Debarati Sanyal
events.description: Arts of the Border (Fordham, 2025) investigates the consequences of unfolding catastrophes across the world and the displacement they continue to produce. Through recent narratives and media representations of the refugee "crisis" at Europe's edges, it tells a new story about those on the move, the technologies unleashed on them at borders, the racialized and colonial histories that inform these technologies, and the artistry with which migrants and allies bear witness to displacement. The book reorients us toward the creativity and movement of migrants themselves — their "arts of the border" — as well as toward the political force of the arts that represent them, whether in literature, documentary film, or art installations.Debarati Sanyal (French) proposes kino-aesthetics as a framework for capture and fugitivity at borders. From kino (to set in motion) and aesthetics (relating to sensory perception), kino-aesthetics conveys the force of bodies in motion and the image in its circulation. Sanyal examines the simultaneity of capture and escape at thresholds of illegalization, from airport detention zones to Calais's "jungle" and the Euro-African border at Ceuta and Melilla. What emerges throughout these case studies is a portrayal of border violence in its racial and colonial forms as well as an archive of refusal, fugitivity, and un-bordered imagining. Sanyal is joined by Damon Young (Film & Media and French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten: Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization Abstract Classical hypothesis testing frameworks break down in contemporary settings in which null hypotheses are increasingly abstract, the same data are used to both generate and test hypotheses, and minimal assumptions about the underlying data are made. In this work, we propose a new framework for conducting valid hypothesis tests in broad contexts. We propose to add and subtract external noise generated from a symmetric shift-family to our data, X, to partition it into two pieces, X1 and X2. We provide a generic strategy for orthogonalizing X2 against X1 under the null hypothesis H0, then show that testing whether the orthogonalization was successful provides a valid test of H0 under mild assumptions. Remarkably, this framework extends naturally to the post-selection inference setting with minimal modifications: we simply select a hypothesis on X1, then perform orthogonalization under the selected null. As our approach neither requires pre-specification of the selection mechanism, nor is restricted to a small class of data-generating distributions, it dramatically expands the settings for which valid post-selection inference can be conducted. We showcase the flexibility of our proposal in a number of case studies. This is joint work with Ameer Dharamshi (McGill University) and Runjia Zou (University of Washington). Bio Daniela Witten is a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at University of Washington, and the Dorothy Gilford Endowed Chair in Mathematical Statistics. She develops statistical machine learning methods for high-dimensional data, with a focus on unsupervised learning. She has received a number of awards for her research in statistical machine learning: most notably the Spiegelman Award from the American Public Health Association for a (bio)statistician under age 40, and the Presidents' Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies for a statistician under age 41. Daniela is a co-author of the textbook "Introduction to Statistical Learning", and has served as Joint Editor of Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB (https://climb.berkeley.edu/)), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Heather Christofk: Metabolic Regulation of Cell State
events.description: Our research focuses on the relationship between metabolism and cell state. We began by studying how metabolism changes during different cell state transitions – during malignant transformation, stem cell differentiation, and virus infection. However, our work has suggested a more bidirectional relationship between metabolism and cell state, whereby metabolism is not only altered during cell state transitions, but metabolic changes can also drive them. Here, I will present examples of our recent and ongoing work in three different areas of study: tissue stem cell metabolism, developmental metabolism, and cancer metabolism. I will highlight efforts to translate our findings to the clinic, new tools and methodologies we are developing to better study cell type-specific metabolism in vivo, and new questions we are answering focused on the impact of metabolism on cell state transitions in varied biological contexts.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: (Screening) GAAVANI | Celebrating the Female Voice in Gurbani Kirtan
events.description: Join us for a screening of GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/), a film that marks a significant moment in Sikh history. For the first time in 556 years since the founding of the Sikh faith, 31 women travel across northern India to sing Kirtan in all 31 primary musical raags of the Guru Granth Sahib at sacred sites. This film captures breathtaking cinematography, soul-stirring soundscapes, while exploring how these women serve as vital carriers of wisdom, faith and strength - bringing 556 years of legacy into a sharp, contemporary and lived focus. The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker Navpreet Kaur. The event will be moderated by Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh), the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, September 17, 2026 TIME: 5-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall REGISTRATION: The event is FREE but a reservation is required. Please reserve your seat HERE (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/gaavani-film-california-premiere-rsvp-berkeley-tickets-1994097467204?aff=oddtdtcreator) —————-SYNOPSIS:GAAVANI: Her Journey Home (https://www.gaavani.com/) follows a diverse group of 31 women—teachers, students, mothers, and community members—as they journey across northern India to perform Kirtan in the 31 primary raags of the Guru Granth Sahib. From the busy streets of Delhi to historic shrines in Amritsar and beyond, the film captures both the challenges and triumphs of this groundbreaking effort. The film explores the relationship between practice, music, gender, and lived spiritual experience. Featuring insights from scholars and speakers such as Dr. Gurnam Singh and Jessi Kaur, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) reflects on the "female orientation" of the soul in Sikh philosophy and highlights the deep spiritual significance of sung devotion. As a legacy project, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) seeks to inspire Sikh children and adults to discover their own musical connection to Gurbani Kirtan and to help ensure that this sacred art form continues to thrive for future generations. events.title: A Roundtable on the History of the Far-Right in the US
events.description: Over the past decade, the far right has moved from the margins of American politics to its center. In turn, the topic now transcends the margins of historical scholarship to become a thriving field of inquiry. This roundtable brings together contributors to the Journal of Right-Wing Studies' two-part special issue, "The Far Right in US History (https://jrws.berkeley.edu/issues)," to discuss recent discoveries in the field. Drawing on work that spans conservative Catholic political thought, maternal activism on the right, the transnational circulation of white supremacist violence, Klan electoral politics, American monarchism, and the deep roots of Christian nationalism, panelists will consider what is gained by treating the far right as a subject of history rather than a contemporary aberration, and what remains stubbornly hard to study. How do historians define the "far right?" When does the radical become ordinary? And what do the archives allow us to see about movements with few formal records? Please join Professors Olivier Burtin (Université de Picardie Jules Verne) and Kathryn Olmsted (UC Davis), our distinguished guest editors, as they moderate a discussion on topics in the special issue. Authors and Discussants: -Mary Byrne (Rutgers) - "Moms for Liberty and the Legacy of White Maternalist Activism: Gendered Power and Cultural Organizing in Far-Right Movements" -Faith Lazar (Yale) - "If a Bomb Goes Off in the Woods: Preemptive Counterterrorism and the FBI Sting that Triggered Ruby Ridge" -Kyle Burke (University of South Florida) - "'A Planet-Wide Race War': The Global Circulation of White Supremacist Violence in the Late Twentieth Century" -Chelsea Ebin (Drew) - "Mapping the Influence of Conservative Catholic Political Thought on the American Right" Part 1 of the special issue is available and open access; Look for Part 2, out soon!

events.title: Irregular Labor Supply and Coordination in the Workplace: Experimental Evidence from India | Shreya Chandra
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract This paper studies how irregular labor supply affects the organization of production in the context of a large apparel manufacturing cluster in India. Production is organized as batch processing lines, where tasks are performed sequentially to produce the finished product. In the status quo, workers choose their own work timings, resulting in significant dispersion in arrival times at the firm. I conduct an experiment with 96 small factories comprising 600 workers, where all workers in treatment firms are incentivized to arrive at work by the owner's preferred start time for a period of 4-weeks. Workers are paid a daily bonus equivalent to 20% of average earnings if they arrive on or before the start time. Incentives increase timely arrival in treatment firms by 43% relative to control firms. These changes are driven by workers who were consistently late to arrive at the firm at baseline. As a result, there is meaningful improvement in coordination of worker arrival times – dispersion in arrival times decreases by 17%. Individual worker output increase for all workers in treatment firms, not only those who changed their arrival times as a result of the incentive. I show that these positive spillovers are generated through gains along the production line from improved coordination. Weekly firm output increases by 29% and delays in order-completion fall by 13 percentage points.

events.title: Film Screening "Contempt"
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director. - Judy Bloch

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (daj@math.ku.dk) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z _2 $- graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting, Wasserstein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans on tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: Vivien Schmidt | The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis—and its applications to Europe
events.description: Vivien Schmidt's new book, The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) provides a sweeping appraisal of how ideas and discourse are used by policymakers and everyday citizens to understand the world, communicate with one another, and mobilize for collective action. It illustrates using examples of scholarly work on capitalism and democracy, international diplomacy and human rights, environmental, economic, and social policy, conservativism, neoliberalism, socialism, and populism. In so doing, the book also provides a discursive institutionalist perspective on the (constructivist) nature of meaning, the dynamics of change and the exercise of power. At a time of major political upheaval, with populism and authoritarianism on the rise, understanding agents' ideas and discourse is even more essential today than ever. The talk will illustrate with examples from the European Union and Europe more generally, both in terms of substantive issues and methodological approaches.Vivien A. Schmidt is Jean Monnet Professor of European Integration, Professor Emerita of International Relations and Political Science, and Founding Director of the Center for the Study of Europe at Boston University. She is Visiting Fellow at the European University Institute and Honorary Professor at LUISS University. Recent books include The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) and the award-winning Europe's Crisis of Legitimacy: Governing by Rules and Ruling by Numbers in the Eurozone (Oxford 2020). Schmidt is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Chevalier in the French Legion of Honor, and a recipient of the Lifetime Achievement Award of the European Union Studies Association, an Honorary Doctorate from the Free University of Brussels, and a Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship. events.title: Polly Fordyce: "Using microfluidics for high-throughput and quantitative biophysics and biochemistry"
events.description: Macromolecular interactions drive all biological processes: proteins bind DNA and RNA to regulate transcription and translation, dense networks of protein-protein interactions convey cellular signals, and enzyme-substrate interactions allow all of the chemical transformations essential for metabolism and signaling. The strength of these interactions predicts the timing and identity of downstream responses; therefore, quantitative biophysical and biochemical measurements are critical to decipher these networks, predict how they are disrupted in disease, and manipulate them for therapeutic purposes. Here, I will discuss the development of and results from several new microfluidic platforms that make it possible to acquire quantitative biochemical and biophysical data in vitro for thousands to millions of sequence variants in parallel.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "House Prices and Quantities Around the World"
events.description: Abstract: We establish several first-order facts using house price and quantity data for middle- and high-income countries. First, housing units and rooms per person rise with per capita income and then asymptote so that additional increases in income are uncorrelated with housing quantities. Second, growth in housing units is strongly correlated with population growth at all income levels. Third, real house prices and housing expenditure shares rise in near-constant proportion with per capita income. A model with non-homothetic demand for home space, homothetic demand for housing quality, and upward-sloping supply of the unit-quality housing bundle can explain these relationships. A standard model where unit-supply is increasingly inelastic does not match the facts.

events.title: Black Critical Theory Initiative: Cecilio M. Cooper
events.location: 820 Social Sciences Building, the Social Sciences Matrix
events.description: "'Seeing Hints of a Trans Fella': Holotypic Black Feminisms, Stereoscopic Transantagonisms" Impelled by Hortense Spillers' and Sylvia Wynter's interventions, the 'black female', 'black woman', 'black femme', 'black feminine,' 'black girl', 'black mother', 'bulldagger', and so on have become valorized topics of gender analysis while also being intermittently leveraged to camouflage collusion with negrophobic antitrans retrenchment. Suffering deemed intrinsic to both structural emplotment beneath these specific racial headings and the sex-gender binary writ large has long been narrated as stemming from black experiences with coercive masculinization. This talk not only critically appraises black transmasculinity's aporetic function for cis-aspirant parsings of black female/woman from black male/man. Via psychosexual questions about aesthetics, taxonomy, and visuality, it likewise contends with the ways black transmasculinity and black trans manhood have been deployed as foils to ideal trans(gender) subjectivity.Cecilio M. Cooper's first monograph examines the occulted roles blackness and darkness play throughout the visual cultures of alchemy and demonology while the second contends with depictions of black transmasculinity across art and media. They have held postdoctoral fellowships in History of Science at the Science History Institute's Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry and in History of Art at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. Their research has also been previously supported by Long-Term fellowships from the Folger Shakespeare Library, National Endowment for the Humanities, and American Antiquarian Society. Alongside their scholarship and criticism, Cooper's creative practice draws from performance, moving image, and sculpture. They completed a PhD with distinction in Black Studies and a Graduate Certificate in Critical Theory from Northwestern University as well as an MA in Performance Studies with a Designated Emphasis in Feminist Theory & Research from the University of California-Davis.

events.title: Ariel Tang | Scripting Silence: Animals Political and Unpolitical in Charlotte Beradt's Dreamscape
events.description: This talk features the implicit dialogue between the German-Jewish journalist Charlotte Beradt (1907-1986) and her fellow émigré, Hannah Arendt, regarding the boundaries between humans and animals, as well as the ethical limits of anthropocentrism during political crises. Beradt's Third Reich of Dreams, a catalogue of dreams compiled between 1933 and 1939 on the basis of dreams retold by more than fifty Germans living under totalitarian rule, prompts her readers to re-evaluate the unique traits of physiological activities such as dreaming—as opposed to discursive reasoning—in safeguarding the humane promise of politics. While conventional pictures of human nature often fall prey to naturalistic or essentialist tendencies, the vital dialogue between Beradt and Arendt helps to resuscitate the unmistakable normative value of anthropological evidence, the substance of which often escapes the immediate capture of language and yet preserves the hope for political renewal lost in effable experience. Ariel Tang is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University. Her research focuses on Enlightenment political thought and its legacies, with special attention to questions related to knowledge institutions, education, and the interactions between culture and nature. Her current book manuscript traces an entangled history of the idea of Bildung and the rise of the modern research university. She received her bachelor's degree in Philosophy from Barnard College, Columbia University, and her PhD in Political Science from Yale University. events.title: PMB Seminar with Lila Fishman | The genomics of multi-trait adaptation to Yellowstone's geothermal soil mosaic in monkeyflowers
events.description: Environmental mosaics can generate strong divergent selection on plant traits even in the face of cross- habitat gene flow, leading to microgeographic local adaptation and (perhaps) incipient speciation. Here, we use yellow monkeyflower adaptation to the fine-scaled yet physically-extreme mosaic of soil conditions in the geyser basins of Yellowstone National Park to explore fundamental questions about the genomic and molecular mechanisms of adaptation to extreme conditions. For two traits with simple genetic bases (trichome density and minimum critical photoperiod for flowering), candidate variants in predictable molecular pathways underlie dramatic phenotypic divergence over a 100m scale gradient. In contrast, a novel multi-gene locus (out6 supergene) co-ordinates plant architecture and phenological traits underlying a unique-to-Yellowstone thermal annual strategy. The out6 locus draws on both old (but novel relative to known life-history polymorphisms) standing variation and recent introgression to confer adaptation to extreme thermal soils, and contains several strong functional candidates. Finally, although Yellowstone thermal annuals are highly specialized to the unique niche created by winter snowmelt on hot soils, thus escaping summer's deadly heat and drought, they have also evolved remarkable xylem drought/heat resistance. Together, these instances of extreme local adaptation provide a composite picture of how different plant traits and pathways evolve in response to novel environments.

events.title: Sappho and Critical Theory
events.description: Taking inspiration from the Sapphic collages of Lynne Huffer on display at the Townsend Center through May 2027, this symposium gathers together scholars working at the intersection of philosophy, literature, and creative practice. Speakers reflect on the ways in which Sappho and the Sapphic tradition have contributed in subterranean ways to counterintuitive modes of thinking — and thus to the radical work of critical theory, broadly defined. Because so little of her work survives intact, Sappho has long been particularly available for reinterpretation. Engaging with this rich field of possibility, panelists ask: can we see Sappho as a philosopher or critical theorist who preemptively contests the all-male tradition that brackets her in the domain of ancient poetry? Can we approach her oeuvre as a practice of feminist and transfeminist production that problematizes the very distinction between poetry and philosophy? How does an approach that emphasizes the discontinuous and fragmentary state of the archive change our perceptions of Sappho — such as her traditional association with Victorian and post-Victorian models of white lesbianism? How can a fresh return to Sappho help us navigate a moment in which gender is increasingly entangled with fear, anxiety, and political contestation? Following the symposium, audience members are invited to the Townsend Center for a reception to celebrate the opening of the exhibition, Thinking with Sappho: Lynne Huffer and the Art of Collage. Participants:Judith Butler, UC BerkeleyPenelope Deutscher, Northwestern UniversityLynne Huffer, Emory UniversityRanjana Khanna, Duke UniversitySalar Mamemi, UC BerkeleyVictoria Rimell, University of WarwickMario Telò, UC Berkeley

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu (mailto:naomiy@berkeley.edu) or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

Her research program integrates basic, translational, and clinical investigation to advance precision medicine for patients with chronic liver disease. events.title: Maayan Levy: Toward the development of metabotherapy
events.description: Diet can be a powerful, low-cost lever for treating disease. We previously showed that a ketogenic diet suppresses intestinal tumorigenesis in mouse models of colorectal cancer, mediated by the metabolite beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) acting through HCAR2 to induce the differentiation factor HOPX (Dmitrieva-Posocco et al., Nature, 2022). A follow-up trial in Lynch syndrome patients confirmed that BHB supplementation reduces colonic epithelial proliferation, and a clinical trial for colorectal cancer prevention is now underway (NCT05338307). We asked whether the same metabolite could address a different problem: CAR T cell therapy fails in roughly half of patients and rarely works in solid tumors. Screening diets in mouse lymphoma models, we found that a ketogenic diet- again acting through BHB- potentiates CAR T cell function, fueling the TCA cycle and reprogramming T cells away from exhaustion toward a more cytotoxic state. BHB supplementation alone dramatically improved tumor clearance and survival in lymphoma and solid tumor models, and enhanced T cell metabolic fitness in healthy human volunteers, motivating an ongoing Phase I trial combining BHB with CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma patients. Together, this work suggests that a single, inexpensive dietary metabolite can be repurposed across cancer prevention and immunotherapy to meaningfully improve patient outcomes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Lecture | Taking God Seriously in Modern Islamic Politics: Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), Science, and Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt
events.description: Abstract: In his new book, Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt, Arthur Zárate argues that although God stands at the center of contemporary Muslim moral and political visions, the deity's presence is often neglected in scholarship. This talk explores why that neglect persists and what comes into focus when theological claims are taken seriously in the study of modern Islamic politics. Focusing on the Egyptian theologian Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), it examines his engagements with modern scientific discourses to show how science became one avenue through which divine presence was encountered and affirmed. Debates over science, it argues, were simultaneously debates about God, and competing understandings of the natural world underwrote competing visions of political and social reform. Ultimately, the talk proposes "activist theology" as a more adequate framework than "Islamism" for understanding al-Ghazali's politics.Bio: Arthur Zárate is a historian of the modern Middle East whose research explores the intersections of politics, science, and theology in modern Islam. He is the author of Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2025). His work has appeared in Comparative Studies in Society and History and the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, and is forthcoming in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. He is Assistant Professor of Global Humanities at San José State University, where he teaches in the Honors Humanities Program. He is currently writing a second book on Sufism, spiritual experimentation, and Muslim and Coptic saintly mediation in modern Egypt.

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR
