Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. The English edition of The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future is available for download for free at the following link for those who are interested: https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ (https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ) Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A. He is a Board Member of Hanyang Eng Co., a major KOSDAQ-listed semiconductor and high-tech facility engineering firm, and currently serves as a policy advisor to South Korea's National Economic Advisory Council.

events.title: Julia Nelsen | Translation as Rediscovery: Introducing Fausta Cialente
events.description: Fausta Cialente (1898-1994) was one of Italy's most significant twentieth-century authors. Though she won critical acclaim—albeit late in her career—Cialente remained overlooked for decades until the recent rerelease of her literary works in Italian. A Very Cold Winter (Transit Books, 2026) is the first of Cialente's novels to be rediscovered in translation by Julia Nelsen. In conversation with Professor Mairi McLaughlin, Nelsen will discuss her translation of A Very Cold Winter, situate Cialente within the broader landscape of modern Italian and international literature, and explore the role translators play in recovering unsung voices.Julia Nelsen translates between English and Italian. In addition to her work on Fausta Cialente, her essays and translations have appeared in journals including Circumference, Two Lines,Firmament, and the Chicago Review. Alongside translation, she currently serves as policy analyst for the UCLA Academic Senate, and previously taught writing and literature courses and managed international partnerships between Europe and the West Coast. She holds a PhD in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley and a Masters in European languages from the University of Milan.Mairi McLaughlin is Professor and Chair in the Department of French and an Affiliated Member of the Departments of Linguistics and Italian Studies at UC Berkeley. She specializes in French/Romance Linguistics and in Translation Studies and has published extensively on language contact, the language of the media, and journalistic and literary translation. Her books have been published by Garnier, Legenda, and Oxford University Press, and she has published articles in journals such as French Studies, The Italianist, Langages, META, Perspectives, and Target.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.description: Join the Goldman School of Public Policy for an in-person conversation with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski, one of the Senate's most independent voices and a leading voice on political leadership and bipartisan governance in an era of deep political polarization. Over more than two decades in the U.S. Senate, Murkowski has helped shape some of the nation's most consequential policy debates while earning a reputation for independence, institutional stewardship, and a willingness to challenge presidents and party leaders alike. Drawing on her memoir, Far From Home: An Alaskan Senator Faces the Extreme Climate of Washington, D.C., she will reflect on the defining moments of her career, the evolution of American politics, and what it means to govern with conviction in a divided democracy. The discussion will explore Murkowski's journey from Alaska to the U.S. Senate, her historic 2010 write-in reelection campaign, and the transformation of American politics from the Tea Party era to today. As institutions face growing public scrutiny and political divisions continue to deepen, she will offer a candid perspective on the challenges confronting American democracy, the future of bipartisan governance, and the role of political leadership and public service in sustaining democratic institutions.This event is part of the Goldman School of Public Policy's Democracy Book Club series, which features authors whose work enriches our understanding of democracy by examining the institutions, policies, and civic traditions that shape democratic life. —Lisa Murkowski is a third-generation Alaskan proudly serving as the state's senior senator. Since joining the U.S. Senate in 2002, she has earned a reputation for her collaborative approach and her ability to work across the aisle to reach commonsense solutions. She and her husband live in Anchorage, Alaska, where they raised their two sons.David C. Wilson is the dean of the Goldman School of Public Policy and a Professor of Public Policy at the University of California, Berkeley. A leading scholar of political psychology and public opinion, his research explores race, democracy, and political behavior. Before joining Berkeley, he held senior academic leadership roles at the University of Delaware and worked with the Gallup Polling Organization. Wilson is also a U.S. Army veteran who served 19 years in the Army Reserves, including tours during Operations Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom.

events.title: Karen Van Dyck | The Greek Alphabet in America
events.description: Thehistory of Greek assimilationin America can be traced in the slow erasure of Greek as a symbol of difference and indecipherability, the most recognizably unrecognizable alphabet– "It'sallGreek to me!"By the 1930s and 1940s,looking and sounding differentled to thesubstitutionnot only of different faces and races, butoftypefaces. If, during the mid-century, nations were intent on keeping things as separate as possible and popular fiction and film made sure Greeks and Greek in America were erased and monoalphabeticism won out, in the 1970s and 1980s, a more cosmopolitan moment, Greek's indecipherability became the grounds for literary experimentation and, particularly for women writers, a "politics of transliteration."Karen Van Dyck, Kimon A. Doukas Professor of Modern Greek Literature in the Classics Department at Columbia University, works on questions of translation, migration, gender and classical reception. She is the founding director of Hellenic Studies and an active member of the Institute of Comparative Literature and Society and the Istanbul and Athens Global Centers. events.title: Establishing Chronology in Tibetan art: a Study of Taklung Paintings
events.description: This lecture addresses chronology in early Tibetan art. Dr. Casey highlights over a decade of research on a group of approximately 100 paintings from Taklung and Riwoche monasteries in Tibet. The main purpose of the study has been to establish a reliable foundation for assigning dates to Taklung paintings. The Taklung painting corpus particularly lends itself to the task of building a chronology. Almost three-quarters of the paintings bear inscriptions with chronological implications. Using visual lineages (the succession of teachers represented in the top, side, and, occasionally, the bottom registers of paintings), inscriptions, narrative scenes (in which principal structures in the Taklung Monastery compound may be linked to specific dates), and style analysis, the speaker identifies fundamental parameters that help to create firm chronological designations for these c. twelfth to mid-sixteenth century paintings. Tibetan textual historians and historians of Tibetan religion will appreciate the evidentiary underpinnings of the chronology put forth. And anyone interested in understanding the history of Tibetan Buddhist culture will appreciate the wealth of information contained in these remarkable, often very well preserved works of art.Jane Casey is an art historian specializing in Himalayan art. Educated in the History of Science (A.B.) and in Fine Arts (A.M. and Ph.D.) at Harvard University, since 1991 she has worked as an independent art historian, curating exhibitions at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and at Casa Asia, Barcelona. She is a Guest Professor at the Zhejiang University Center for Buddhist Art in Hangzhou, and a Research Fellow in Tibetan Art at the Palace Museum in Beijing. She resides in Marlborough, New Zealand.

events.title: [UC Berkeley campus premiere] A Job in the Shade: The Emily Vasquez Story
events.location: Chevron Auditorium, International House (2299 Piedmont Avenue, Berkeley, CA)
events.description: About the Film This inspiring documentary chronicles the extraordinary life of Judge Emily Vasquez, the first Latina appointed in 2001 to the Sacramento County Superior Court in its history. Through intimate interviews with family members, friends, colleagues, and mentees, A Job in the Shade explores Judge Vasquez's remarkable journey from the agricultural fields of California to the courtroom. The film highlights a lifetime of service, leadership, and mentorship while demonstrating how education can transform lives and expand opportunities for future generations. Through her strength of character, hard work, and keen intellect, Judge Vasquez defied the odds. Judge Vasquez has made it look easy with her many accomplishments but her many achievements did not come easy (not when you one of the first and come from humble beginnings). Her parents were poor, immigrant farmworkers from Mexico. As a child, she lived in labor camps and worked in the fields when school was not in session to help supplement the family income. She spent her early years living in tents and one-bedroom shacks with everyone, including her parents sleeping in the same room as her siblings. The bathroom was an outhouse. From her childhood in California's Central Valley, working alongside her poor farmworker parents, to her groundbreaking legal career, Judge Vasquez's story is one of resilience, determination, and the transformative power of education.Presented by:UC Berkeley Division of Equity & Inclusion Latinx Thriving Initiatives The Spencer Group In partnership with:University Development and Alumni Relations (UDAR) UC Berkeley College of Letters & Science Cal Alumni Association

events.title: Synchro and SimTraffic for Signal Coordination
events.description: Description This four-session online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in Synchro and SimTraffic software and the recently published Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7). Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and virtual computer lab, you will become proficient in the network coding and use of Synchro and SimTraffic for signal optimization and coordination projects. Working on a real-world multi-modal project, students will use Synchro to incorporate a Bing aerial background, add/modify roadways, input intersection geometrics, enter multi-modal traffic volumes (cars, trucks, pedestrians, and bicycles), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. Students will also use Synchro to evaluate and develop optimal signal timing plans that reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. The seamless integration of Synchro with SimTraffic, a microsimulation software, will be used to evaluate intersection operations and compare the differences between "isolated - macro-level" Synchro and "network-wide - micro-level" SimTraffic analysis that is recommended for multi-modal, closely spaced intersections and congested corridors. Lastly, this course will teach you how to review and understand the potential differences in delay, level of service, and queuing analysis when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of Synchro input requirements Developing a Synchro network for a real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using Synchro Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle LOS using HCM 7th Edition Optimizing signal timings for a single intersection that is added to an existing corridor Optimizing signal timings for a group of intersections Seemless Integration of SYNCHRO with SimTraffic SimTraffic Model Calibration and Application What You Will Learn Using a real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they learn how to develop a network and use the Synchro and SimTraffic software. This includes incorporating a Bing aerial background, add/modify straight and curved roadways, inputting intersection geometrics and pocket lengths, entering multi-modal volumes (cars, trucks, peds, and bicyclists), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations analysis for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. You will learn the steps used to optimize and coordinate a group of intersections to reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, you will learn how to review and understand the analysis results and the potential differences when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis for signal coordination projects. The materials in this course are based on the following references:Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022 CUBIC Transportation Systems. Synchro Studio 12 Traffic Signal Software -User Guide, 2024 Who Should Attend No prior experience using Synchro and SimTraffic is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in improving signal system optimization and coordination projects using the integrated Optimization Module in the Synchro software.

events.title: Robert G. Strand | Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism
events.description: Why do the Nordics consistently rank among the world's happiest, most prosperous, and most trusted societies? What lessons might the Nordics offer the United States at a moment when many people feel growing frustration and anxiety about the direction of American capitalism?Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism (2026, Cambridge University Press; open access:https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp (https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp)) by Robert G. Strand explores a simple but urgent idea: capitalism must be rooted in democracy if it is to support freedom, shared prosperity, and sustainability. Drawing on research, lived experience, and comparative analysis between the Nordics and the United States, Strand argues that the Nordic countries offer practical inspiration for reimagining capitalism in the twenty-first century. "Where democracy is in charge of capitalism, the people win. When capitalism is in charge of democracy, the oligarchs win. In this important book, Robert G. Strand shows how democracies can stay in charge. Nordic Capitalism explains that the Nordic nations can be a model for the US, and how democratic capitalism serves the many, not the few." — Robert B. Reich, Former U.S. Secretary of Labor and Professor Emeritus of Public Policy, UC Berkeley Dr. Robert G. Strand is the founding Executive Director of the Nordic Center at UC Berkeley and Executive Director of the Center for Responsible Business at Berkeley Haas, where he serves on the faculty. He is also Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School. His research examines how Nordic societies have organized capitalism and how companies pursue responsible and sustainable business, with attention to applications for reimagining American capitalism. Before joining UC Berkeley in 2014, he served as Assistant Professor at Copenhagen Business School following a decade in corporate America with IBM and Boston Scientific. He received a Ph.D. in Corporate Social Responsibility from Copenhagen Business School, an MBA in International Business from the University of Minnesota, and a B.S. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. He was a U.S. Fulbright Scholar to Norway at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold"
events.description: Abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structural information prior to AlphaFold increases by 23 to 32% relative to proteins that already had a structure, with the effects increasing dramatically over time. This represents a significant shift in the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. By contrast, the response of applied R&D, as measured by patents referencing those proteins, has been far more muted.

events.title: David Szanton | India's Mithila Painting: Home, Rituals and Traditions
events.description: A talk by David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/), President of the Ethnic Art Foundation (EAF) and Former Executive Director of International and Area Studies, UC Berkeley, drawing on his newly edited volume, India's Mithila Painting (https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295753225/indias-mithila-painting/), co-edited with Paula Richman. The presentation will examine the long-term transformation of Mithila painting from a domestic ritual practice into a distinctive indigenous art form characterized by an expanding repertoire of themes, styles, and subjects. Through an illustrated discussion, Szanton will consider the work of contemporary practitioners, focusing on the ways in which established visual forms and stylistic conventions are adapted to address immediate social, cultural, and political concerns. He will also discuss a significant turning point in the late 1960s, when paper became an important medium for Mithila artists, facilitating new modes of production, circulation, and artistic experimentation. The talk will further explore the diversity of artists and stylistic approaches that have emerged over subsequent decades, while highlighting the important role of the Ethnic Art Foundation in supporting artists and advancing the recognition and wider appreciation of Mithila painting.Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Sept 29, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ——��—–About the Book: Since at least the fifteenth century, Hindu women in the Mithila region of northern India have been painting images of deities, flora and fauna symbolizing fertility and prosperity, and floor designs that sacralize sites for ritual within their homes. Their artwork remained ephemeral since its plant-based colors faded over time. In response to an extended drought that led to widespread crop failure in the 1960s, the Indian government's All India Handicraft Board provided high-quality paper to the women of Mithila to test the income-generating possibilities of transferring wall and floor artwork to a new medium. The unique Mithila aesthetic, novel compositions, and precise linework won enthusiastic buyers in New Delhi and abroad. The small number of women painters expanded across the ranks of the social hierarchy and even included a few men. They developed individual styles and depicted novel subjects such as village history, their own life stories, the tsunami in Sri Lanka, social justice, protecting trees, and changing social norms. Major international museums now house Mithila collections, and individuals around the world own paintings. This volume, the first to present an up-to-date analysis of the history and practitioners of Mithila painting, includes contributions from Mithila artists, anthropologists, art historians, historians of Indian religions and specialists of visual culture, gender studies, and translation studies.About the Speaker:David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/) is an American anthropologist renowned for his extensive work in South Asian studies and education policy. Beyond his roles at the Social Science Research Council (SSRC) and the University of California, Berkeley, Szanton has collaborated with several esteemed institutions. He has authoredMithila Painting: The Evolution of an Art Form(2007) andMany Visions, Many Versions: Art from Indigenous Communities in India(2017). In 1971, he served as an assistant to Howard G. Schaller in the Ford Foundation's Southeast Asia office, contributing to the foundation's initiatives in the region. In 1980, Szanton co-founded the Ethnic Arts Foundation (EAF), a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting and supporting Mithila art—a traditional women's art form from the Mithila region of India and Nepal. As president of the EAF, he has been instrumental in fostering cross-cultural understanding and appreciation through the arts. David's enduring commitment to anthropology, education, and the preservation of indigenous art forms underscores his significant contributions to these fields. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Thomas Farber
events.description: Describing America's deeply unsettling current politics, at age eighty-one Thomas Farber (English) explores personal accountability, impending second childhoods, mortality, and the hunger for immortality. Weighing the functions of satire and the meaning of art, his short takes illuminate, debunk, commiserate, and celebrate by rejoinder.Reckonings (El León Literary Arts/Manoa Books, 2026) is framed by two insights: no one chooses to be born, and no one can help being what they are. Reckoning with democracy in crisis, aging and mortality, his career, the role of the writer, and the fate of books, Farber reflects on endings with curiosity, honesty, wit, and compassion. Reckonings is the latest in a series of remarkable creative memoirs he has written over the past decade, coming to terms with life and its limits. Farber is joined by Sam Otter (English). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Welfare Effects of Information Provision on Environmental Externalities | Zac Pond
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract Information provision is frequently used to motivate prosocial behavior, yet its impacts on welfare are rarely measured. I study these impacts by combining a signaling model with a series of randomized experiments on personal carbon emissions. The model generates predictions for how information provision can directly affect consumer welfare by altering the relationship between emissions and inferred altruistic type. I implement three interventions, two that provide participants with private information about their emissions and one that publicly reveals them, and measure their welfare effects with an incentive-compatible willingness to pay elicitation. The private information interventions are positive-sum in consumer welfare, whereas public recognition is negative-sum. Nevertheless, 16 to 25 percent of participants pay to avoid receiving private information. Under public recognition, relatively high emitters incur significant utility losses while relatively low emitters receive no gains. I use these estimates to compare the social efficiency of different forms of information provision on externalities.

events.title: Carla Shatz & Corey Goodman Lectureship Series with Dr. Erin Schuman
events.description: The Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute (HWNI) are delighted to announce the 2026 Carla Shatz & Corey Goodman Lectureship Series. This event, created through the generosity of co-founding directors of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, Dr. Carla Shatz and Dr. Corey Goodman, will bring outstanding neuroscientists to our campus to share their research and engage with our vibrant, interdisciplinary scientific community, spanning the full breadth of mind and brain science. This year's guest speaker will be Dr. Erin M. Schuman (https://brain.mpg.de/schuman), former Professor and Director of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, Germany, and now Director of University College London Queen Square Institute of Neurology. The Schuman lab's long-standing research interest is the study of cellular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie information processing and storage. The lab focuses on the molecular and cell biological processes that control protein synthesis and degradation in neurons and their synapses. The complex morphology of neurons, with most synapses located hundreds of microns from the cell body, presents a logistical challenge for the establishment, maintenance and modification of local synaptic proteomes. For her groundbreaking work on local protein translation in neurons and the establishment of its importance for brain development and plasticity, Dr. Schuman has been awarded the 2026 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience (https://www.kavliprize.org/bio/erin-schuman). Join us for an inspiring afternoon of conversation and meaningful connections as we delve into the latest advances in neuroscience.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Markus Covert - The E. coli Whole-Cell Modeling Project: Accelerating Discovery via Comprehensive Biological Simulation
events.description: Abstract: Francis Crick first called for a coordinated worldwide scientific effort to determine a "complete solution" of the bacterium Escherichia coli. We have been working for some years now to complete a model of E. coli that takes into account all of the known functions of every well-annotated gene, in order to better understand and predict the behavior of this scientifically-relevant and industrially-significant model organism. Now that a majority of the annotated gene functions have been added to the model, our simulations have generated biological insights that change our perspectives about cellular biology and physiology. As examples, I will present our new findings regarding how metals are utilized in E. coli, as well as the effect of gene organization into operons, and the impact of engineering new gene content into the chromosome.Bio: Markus Covert is the Ram Shriram Chair and Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. Over the course of his career, his lab has generated several new exciting technologies to measure, analyze, and mathematically model the behaviors of individual cells. The lab is probably best known for constructing the first "whole-cell" computational model, which explicitly represents all known gene functions and molecules in a bacterial cell - an advance which was highlighted by the journal Cell as a highlight publication of the 40-year history of that journal. Markus is the author of the textbook Fundamentals of Systems Biology: from Synthetic Circuits to Whole-Cell Models. He has received several awards for his efforts to develop new technologies, in particular the NIH Director's Pioneer Award, and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation Distinguished Investigator and Discovery Center awards. He has also consulted in industry, including on the scientific advisory board of Emerald Cloud Labs, and as an inaugural Ambassador at X Labs, (previously Google [X]). Finally, Markus has taught one of the most popular courses at Stanford for several years, an integrated "lecture, lab and lunch" course entitled Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science of Haute Cuisine.

events.title: Vaṭivam: The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures | A Conference in Tamil Studies
events.description: The Berkeley Tamil Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/berkeley-tamil-initiative) is pleased to present The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies), a Tamil Studies conference exploring vaṭivam—form, shape, style, arrangement, and embodiment—as a way to understand how Tamil narratives are created, circulated, and transformed across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media. More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. By placing premodern and modern materials in conversation, The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies) asks how Tamil traditions can contribute to broader debates on form, media, and circulation, while remaining attentive to the histories, languages, and material contexts that shape Tamil cultural production. Conference led by Vasugi Kailasam (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/vasugi-kailasam), Assistant Professor of Tamil Studies in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Associate Professor, South & South East Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. events.title: Defending Democracy Online Through Social Media: Deep Fakes and Our Cognitive Security, with Alexa Koenig
events.description: Digital technologies are rapidly transforming how people live their lives, including their access to information. Social media and smartphones are affecting both the creation and consumption of news — trapping consumers in information "silos" that obscure alternate points of view — while deep fakes are threatening the quality of information found online. All of this raises significant risks for the functioning of our democracy. Dr. Alexa Koenig will discuss this new information environment, some of the challenges it poses for democracy — including our sense of cognitive security — and opportunities for uncovering the truth in this digital age.About the Speaker Dr. Alexa Koenig is faculty director of Berkeley's MacArthur-Award Winning Human Rights Center; co-founder of U.C. Berkeley's Investigations Lab; and a research professor at Berkeley Law, where she focuses on the role of new and emerging technologies in human rights research and investigation.

events.title: BWLP PD | Practical Strategies & Real Classroom Impact (Strands A & B)
events.description: Berkeley World Language Project - 2026-2027 LEARN | CONNECT | INSPIREJoin us for a year of learning in community! Practical Strategies & Real Classroom Impact Engaging Workshops: Practical ideas you can use right away Supportive Community: Collaborate with educators who inspire Student Success: Build world language skills that last Office Hours: Collaborate between workshop sessions! Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! This strand is for all language teachers who want to take their instruction to the next level, whether beginning or experienced. You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. You will build a complete Lesson over time while learning and practicing strategies to implement immediately. Prerequisite: an open mind, curiosity, and a desire to grow. Strand B: Creating Authentic Themed Units for Today's Learners Develop meaningful, real-life themed Units for modern language learners. Build a thematic unit grounded in authentic materials that reflect real language and culture. You will learn how to design a unit that aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), AP themes and CA World Languages Standards while integrating global competence, social justice, and social-emotional learning. Using backward design, you'll craft essential questions, Can-Do statements, and assessments that support meaningful communication across all modes—creating immersive, relevant learning experiences that connect students to the real world and help them grow as confident, culturally aware language users. Prerequisite: Strand A or equivalent recommended. events.title: Roadway Geometric Design in California
events.description: Description This dynamic three-day, in-person course provides a deep dive into the principles and best practices of roadway geometric design in California. Built for professionals looking to strengthen or refresh their roadway design knowledge and expertise, the course begins with the latest transportation planning perspectives and emerging multimodal design philosophies that prioritize safety, mobility, and accessibility for all road users. Students will work directly with the industry's most essential design resources, including the Caltrans Highway Design Manual (HDM), the AASHTO Greenbook, PROWAG, the 2026 California MUTCD, and other key state, federal, and local guidelines. Through real world examples, students will learn how to apply geometric design principles to evaluate constraints, solve design challenges, and develop context sensitive solutions for various design projects. This fast-paced, interactive course blends expert instruction, case studies, group problem solving, and hands-on exercises modeled on real projects. Students are expected to have prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, and familiarity with the HDM, AASHTO, and CA MUTCD. Key Topics IncludeGeometric Design Basics & Planning Context Modern Design Philosophy for All Users Design Standards & Guidance (HDM, AASHTO, NACTO, PROWAG, CAMUTCD) Traffic Operations: LOS, Capacity, and VMT Roadway Segment Design (Cross Sections, Profiles, Drainage, Superelevation) Horizontal & Vertical Curve Design Sight Distance Fundamentals (Stopping, Passing, Intersection, Ped/Bike) Intersection Design (Radii, Turn Pockets, Curb Ramps, Signals, Roundabouts) Bikeway Design (Class I-IV Facilities) Pedestrian Facilities Design & Accessibility (ADA/PROWAG) Temporary Traffic Control & Work Zone Design Freeway Design Elements (Interchanges, Merge/Diverge, Mainline) What You Will Learn Students will gain a strong understanding of the principles and best practices of geometric design across multiple roadway functional classes, along with the external factors that influence design decisions. Who Should Attend This course is intended for transportation engineers and technicians who have some basic prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, as well as for those more experienced who seek a refresher course. Requirements A laptop computer is not required but is encouraged for group exercises and individual break-out sessions. Participants should bring a pencil, pen, notebook, and engineer's scale for in-class exercises, and are encouraged to print out the course materials (electronic PDF to be provided) prior to the class.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, October 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. Take public transportation if possible or arrive early to secure your spot.DIRECTIONS (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/contactsdirections) We are located at 10 Stephens Hall on UC Berkeley's campus. Please click this Google Maps Link (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+Berkeley,+CA/@37.8712099,-122.3278764,12z/data=!4m9!4m8!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952!3e0) and enter your point of departure.

events.title: Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive
events.description: n her new book, Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive, Na'ama Rokem investigates written exchanges by a range of literary twentieth century authors, including Hannah Arendt, Gershom Scholem, Yehuda Amichai, Ludwig Strauss, Erich Auerbach, Walter Benjamin, Leah Goldberg, Peter Szondi, Paul Celan, and Tuvia Ruebner. This remarkable bilingual archive encompasses not only letters but also drafts, reviews, and other ephemeral documents. Written in German and Hebrew, these documents were sent to and from Jerusalem, primarily in the decades following 1948. The writers at the center of Rokem's study contend with the genocidal violence that brought the rich historical relation between German and Hebrew to a seeming end. They also grapple, in different ways, with the new reality in Israel/Palestine in the wake of the founding of the State of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba. The bilingual conversation that crosses over between German and Hebrew in these letters thus centers around the question of Jewish fate in the twentieth century and is immersed in negotiations about Jewish nationalism, the Zionist movement, and the possibilities of Jewish poetry. In the space between German and Hebrew, Rokem argues, the protagonists of her study articulate forms of ambivalence and doubt that remain absent from their published writings. In this book presentation, Rokem will discuss forms of belonging and resistance that emerged in relation to the Zionist movement throughout the twentieth century, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of Jewish nationalism and its discontents.To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/5p6thMQDtfz5LarP8)Na'ama Rokem teaches Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of Chicago, where she has served as director of the Joyce Z. and Jacob Greenberg Center for Jewish Studies and as chair of the Department of Comparative Literature. Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive (University of Chicago Press, 2026) is her second book. Her first book, Prosaic Conditions: Heinrich Heine and the Spaces of Zionist Literature, was published by Northwestern University Press in 2013. It uses the case of the reception and translation of the works of German-Jewish poet Heinrich Heine to argue that prose - as a figure of thought, a mode and a medium - played an instrumental role in the literary foundations of the Zionist revolution. Currently, she is working as one of the co-editors of the forthcoming Volume IV.2 of the Critical Edition of the Complete Works of Hannah Arendt (https://hannah-arendt-edition.net/index.html?lang=en) (Essays and Short Writings on Jewish Politics) and starting a new research project on Zionism and pedagogy. Rokem has been involved in a number of collaborative projects, including The Quest for Modern Language: Between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/the-quest-for-modern-language-between-the-mediterranean-and-black-sea-1820-1948#:~:text=This%20is%20a%20collaborative%2C%20multidisciplinary,19th%20and%20early%2020th%20centuries.), and Translation Networks and the Stakes of Comparison: Convergences and Crossings Between Arabic and Hebrew (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/translation-networks), both sponsored by the Neubauer Collegium on Culture and Society at the University of Chicago, and the Oak Woods Cemetery (https://www.oakwoodsproject.org/) project, a public history initiative that uses a historic cemetery in Woodlawn as a site for teaching, programming, and researching the history of the South Side of Chicago, with a particular interest in the complexly intertwined histories of African Americans and Jews in the city. This project has received funding from the NEH, the Mellon Foundation, and the Women's Board at the University of Chicago. ��� If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible. Thank you.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Leonardo Martinez: "Tuberculosis Risk During Pregnancy and Postpartum Among Women With HIV in Kenya"
events.description: Leo Martinez is an assistant professor in the Division of Epidemiology at the UC Berkeley School of Public Health. He studies the epidemiology of tuberculosis and other infectious diseases, with a focus on how social, biological, and programmatic factors shape who becomes infected, who develops disease, and who experiences long-term health consequences. Dr. Martinez uses epidemiologic, statistical, and quantitative approaches to study tuberculosis transmission and prevention in high-burden settings and among populations at elevated risk, including children, people living with HIV, people with diabetes, and incarcerated populations. Much of his work centers on early-life risk factors for pediatric tuberculosis, the role of nutrition and growth in tuberculosis risk, tuberculosis transmission in congregate settings, and the relationship between tuberculosis and chronic disease outcomes. His research is highly collaborative and is conducted with colleagues and public health partners in the United States and globally, including in South Africa, Kenya, Brazil, China, and Indonesia. Through these partnerships, his work aims to produce evidence that can inform tuberculosis prevention policy, improve screening and treatment strategies, and reduce disparities in tuberculosis burden. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Dr. Martinez was a faculty member in the Department of Epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health.

events.title: Disasters of Biblical Proportions: Reimagining the Ten Plagues in the Age of Covid and October 7
events.description: The biblical story of the ten plagues, the series of disasters sent against Pharaoh and the Egyptian in order to compel them to free the Israelites, introduced into collective imagination a connection between disaster and justice. In this presentation, StevenWeitzman will explore how Jews, Christians and Muslims have reimagined the biblical story to make sense of the disasters and injustices of their own age, focusing on how the story has been reshaped in the wake of the traumatic events and protests that have unfolded since October 7, 2023.To register for this event, please click this link.Steven Weitzman serves as the Ella Darivoff Director of the Herbert D. Katz Center for Advanced Judaic Studies at the University of Pennsylvania as well as the Abraham M. Ellis Professor of Semitic Languages and Literatures in the Department of Religious Studies. His previous academic roles include directing Stanford's Taube Center for Jewish Studies. Recent publications include The Origin of the Jews: the Search for Roots in a Rootless Age; the coedited Princeton Companion to Jewish Studies; Disasters of Biblical Proportions: the Ten Plagues Then, Now, and at the End of the World (the basis of this talk); and The Jews: a History, co-written with John Efron and Matthias Lehmann and now in its fourth edition.

events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— Full program will be available later this spring — The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place — as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: 2026 Gerald D. Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. events.title: Matthew Shutzer | Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis
events.description: A talk by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, on his new book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691265919/until-the-last-ton?srsltid=AfmBOorxSc-xwrFM8YrmGZbYMJ4vEm3ZcucGahHadYBaRZA9ySGhXWds), a panoramic historical account of India's ascent in the global fossil economy. Event moderated by Sharad Chari (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-sharad-chari), Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 8, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.About the Author:Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. It traces India's rise as a world-leading fossil economy in the twentieth century and examines the processes of empire, capitalism, and agroecological change that shaped this transformation. The book moves beyond the prevailing focus in the environmental history of energy on production and consumption, offering instead a longer-term perspective on land, subsurface property rights, geological knowledge, and mining conflicts. In doing so, it reveals the central role of agrarian development in shaping India's trajectory of fossil fuel dependence. Shutzer is currently working on a second book project examining climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945. Before joining the History Department at UC Berkeley, Shutzer taught as an Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Duke University. He previously served as a Junior Scholar at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University and as an S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup Fellow in Natural Resource Economics and Political Economy in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. He has also worked as a researcher on several projects related to the implementation of India's Forest Rights Act in western Odisha. Along with Rebecca Herman, Rebecca McLennan, and Bernadette Perez, Shutzer is one of the faculty conveners of the Berkeley Workshop on Environmental History, based in UC Berkeley's Department of History. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies with Selina Makana
events.description: Materialist Nationalism: Challenging the Heroic Masculinist Rendering of the Nation Nation building exists in an uneasy and fraught relationship with women. On the one hand, nations revere women for their social reproductive labor. In twentieth-century Africa, nationalist movements deployed the figure of "Mama Africa" to galvanize the masses for the fight for independence. On the other hand, women and girl women's bodies were used as battlefields in wars and political repression in the colonial and postcolonial period, albeit in different ways. This lecture focuses on Selina Makana's new book, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (https://www.ohioswallow.com/9780821426739/beyond-the-battlefield/), to examine the meanings and complexities of Angolan women's lived experience of war and militarism and reveal the extraordinary means by which they contend with and contest the politics of the nation. Selina Makana is an Assistant Professor of African history at the University of Memphis. Her research and teaching interests focus on African history, gender and militarism, and African diaspora studies. Her first monograph, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (Ohio University Press, 2026), probes the relationship between women, war, and nationalist politics in Angola. She is currently working on her second book project Paranoia and Pathology in the Colony: Hygiene, Health, and Colonial Governance in Early Twentieth-Century Angola, that examines the entwined histories of public health and colonial governance in Angola. She has published articles in Meridians: Feminism, Race, Transnationalism; Gender and History; and The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African Women's History.

events.title: Indranil Chakravarty | The Power of Intercultural Dialogue: Octavio Paz between Mexico and India
events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, based on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange.Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. His earlier book publications include The New Latin American Cinema, India's Audiovisual Market, and one in Spanish titled Redescubriendo a Tagore. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Gautam Dantas | Understanding, Predicting, and Remediating Perturbations to Host-Microbe Interactions
events.description: Antibiotics can acutely and persistently compromise microbiome stability and resilience, enabling enhanced colonization of pathogenic microbes, and loss of host-beneficial functions from depleted commensals. We interrogate resistome, taxonomic, and functional dynamics of microbiota of humans, animals, soils, and built-environments via high-throughput functional metagenomic selections, whole metagenome and transcriptome sequencing, and isolate phenotyping and whole genome sequencing. We use these datasets to model and predict the impact of various biotic and abiotic perturbations on the transmission and evolutionary dynamics of diverse microbiomes and their resistomes across time and habitats, through application of generalized linear mixed models and machine learning algorithms. By integrating community-level analyses of microbiome perturbation and response, with mechanistic analyses of novel microbial resilience functions, we are improving the accuracy and sensitivity of genomics-based methods for diagnosing and treating pathogens and their resistance properties in the clinic and maintaining or rescuing healthy microbiome states.

events.title: Aaron Gitler: Granulin loss and TMEM106B risk converge on lysosomal C-terminal fragment pathology in frontotemporal dementia
events.description: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN, which encodes progranulin, are a major cause of FTD. Common genetic variants in the TMEM106B gene modify risk of FTD and the effect is especially strong in GRN mutation carriers. Intriguingly, in GRN mutation carriers, being homozygous for the protective TMEM106B haplotype seems to confer near lifetime protection against FTD. Despite the strong genetic link between GRN and TMEM106B, how these two genes interact mechanistically has remained unresolved. Recent studies have revealed that a C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B forms amyloid fibrils and accumulates in the brains of older individuals and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, including FTD. How the production of this fragment connects to granulin deficiency is also unknown. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation, we show that granulin deficiency drives the accumulation of the TMEM106B C-terminal fragment within lysosomes in Grn-knockout mice and GRN-null human iPSC-derived neurons. Recombinant progranulin supplementation reduced TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation. Isogenic neurons carrying the TMEM106B risk allele displayed allele-dose-dependent fragment accumulation that was reversible by progranulin. Structural and genetic analyses demonstrated that TMEM106B dimerization stabilizes the protein and limits C-terminal fragment formation. These findings define a lysosomal pathway linking granulin deficiency to TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation and explain how protective TMEM106B alleles can confer resistance to FTD, even for GRN mutation carriers.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: Merck Banyu Seminar
events.description: Harunobu Mitsunuma, Associate professor, Kobe UniversityDevelopment of catalyst systems enabling sp3 C‒H functionalization reactionsDr. Mitsunuma has made pioneering contributions to catalytic sp³ C–H activation through his development of a cooperative catalyst system in which distinct catalysts operate synergistically. This strategy enabled mild sp³ C–H functionalization that combines high stereocontrol with high functional group compatibility. In particular, his ternary catalytic platform integrating a hydrogen atom transfer catalyst, a metal complex catalyst, and a photoredox catalyst has realized unprecedented transformations, including nucleophilic addition reactions in which simple hydrocarbons serve directly as nucleophiles, as well as highly mild catalytic acceptorless dehydrogenation. Dr. Harunobu Mitsunuma received his Ph.D. from the University of Tokyo in 2015 under the supervision of Professor Motomu Kanai. He subsequently worked as a medicinal chemist at Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma, contributing to early-stage drug discovery. In 2017, he returned to academia as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Tokyo and was promoted to appointed assistant professor in 2018. Since 2022, he has also served concurrently as a PRESTO researcher, further advancing his research program. In 2026, he was appointed as an independent associate professor at the Graduate School of Science, Kobe University.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025).
